title: Astronomer's Notebook: Tycho's Supernova burned brightly in the 1570s
excerpt: The remnants are still visible today through a telescope as race away from the explosion at around 4,500 miles per second.
content:
A ‘new star’ in Cassiopeia

On the night of Nov. 11, 1572, Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe (1546-1601) observed a “new star” inthe constellation Cassiopeia.

According to historical records, the star first appeared on Nov. 2, and by the time that Tycho first saw it, over a week later, it was already as bright as Jupiter.

At its peak, on Nov. 16, the supernova was as bright as Venus and was visible during the daytime.

Tycho made careful observations of the brightness and color of the new star for the next 16 months. It eventually faded to the magnitude of Cassiopeia’s brightest stars and dropped below naked eye visibility in March 1574.

No one at the time could have predicted that Tycho’s observations would forever change not only the course of astronomy but also humankind’s view of the universe.

The changing heavens

Tycho Brahe was born into a Danish family three years after the publication of Copernicus’ “De Revolutionibus.”

He is best known for making detailed naked-eye observations of planets that provided his assistant Johannes Kepler with the basis of his laws of planetary motion decades later.

Tycho attempted to measure the new star’s parallax, a standard procedure employed by astronomers to determine distances of celestial objects.

He found no detectable parallax and therefore concluded that the parallax was too miniscule to measure and hence that the new star must lie beyond the moon.

This was an important result, because it demonstrated that the heavens, which had up until then been regarded as perfect and constant, can indeed undergo changes.

In 1573, Tycho published his observations in an extensive work, De nova et nullius aevi memoria prius visa stella (“Concerning the Star, new and never before seen in the life or memory of anyone”)

Tycho subsequently secured the patronage of King Frederick II of Denmark, thus enabling him to establish a professional observatory on the Danish island of Hven.

For nearly 20 years, the facilities of Hven were employed by Tycho to carry out the most complete and accurate observations made by any pre-telescopic astronomer at that time.

Type Ia supernova

We know today that Tycho’s star was a supernova, now designated SN 1572.

Modern analyses have concluded that this was a Type Ia supernova at approximately 12,000 light years away, which means that ithad a maximum visual luminosity of about 4 billion suns.

A Type Ia supernova occurs when a white dwarf in a binary system pulls in matter from a nearby companion, making the white dwarf increasingly heavier, and the companion lighter.

At some point, the infalling matter onto the white dwarf’s surface pushes its total mass over the 1.4 solar masses, the maximum mass that can sustain a white dwarf, causing it to collapse catastrophically into a tiny neutron star, only about 1/1000th the size of the original white dwarf, accompanied simultaneously by a spectacular supernova explosion, blasting a sizeable fraction of the star’s mass into space.

Incredibly, the explosion is estimated to have released about one-third of a solar mass of iron into the interstellar medium.

Modern observations

The star’s remnant was first detected at radio wavelengths in 1952 by R. Hanbury Brown and Cyril Hazard at Jodrell Bank Observatory in England and was catalogued as 3C10, the tenth object in the third Cambridge catalogue of radio sources.

But most astronomers today refer to it simply as Tycho’s supernova remnant.

The first optical detection of a very faint nebula was made in the 1960s by astronomers at Mount Palomar, and it was later photographed by the international ROSAT spacecraft.

The nebulous remnant of Tycho’s supernova continues to expand outward and has a current diameter of about 20 light years.

Stellar material is still racing away from the explosion at around 4,500 miles per second, or 16 million miles per hour, the highest expansion rate for any observed supernova remnant.

At the edge of the remnant, a shock wave has heated the gas to an inconceivable temperature of 36 million degrees.

The surviving star

In 2004, astronomers claimed to have found the companion star that survived the supernova event over four centuries ago.

The suspect star is of class G2, like our sun, and is named Tycho G. It was most likely an ordinary main sequence, hydrogen-core-burning star before the explosion, but some of its mass was stripped away when its white dwarf sibling exploded.

Tycho G is rocketing across space at three times the speed of other objects in the region, a strong indication that it was flung into space when its white dwarf companion blew up.

Tycho’s supernova in literature

SN 1572 occurred when Shakespeare was only 8 years old, but it may have made enough of an impression on him that it was referred to in Hamlet.

SN 1572 apparently inspired, centuries later, Edgar Allen Poe’s poem “Al Aaraaf.”

And it is also mentioned in Arthur C. Clarke’s 1955 short story, “The Star.” Now four and a half centuries since it occurred, Tycho’s supernova remains an intriguing subject for scientists and writers alike.

Augensen is the director of the Widener University Observatory and emeritus professor of physics and astronomy at Widener University.
